title: Mapping the non-equilibrium interacting Anderson Impurity Model to an effective Gaussian theory
authors: Emmanuel Bogacz, Graham Kells, Andrew K. Mitchell
abstract: Quantum impurity models with strong electron correlations, such as the paradigmatic Anderson Impurity Model (AIM), are central to our understanding of a range of physical phenomena including local moment formation, Coulomb blockade and Kondo screening. They describe magnetic atoms and molecules on surfaces, quantum dot circuits, and correlated materials through dynamical mean field theory. The physics of such systems in strongly non-equilibrium conditions is particularly complex and challenging to capture, whereas Gaussian models of free fermions can be easily solved. Here we show that the time-evolving dynamics of the AIM after a quench can be described by a completely non-interacting version of the model, at the expense of coupling to additional static auxiliary degrees of freedom. Starting from the full solution of the quenched AIM using ED and DMRG, we study the properties of this mapping using numerical optimization, and uncover intriguing structure in the auxiliary system. The method allows us to understand interacting non-equilibrium dynamics through the simpler lens of an effective non-interacting system of larger dimension.
summary: The paper tackles the formidable challenge of simulating strongly correlated systems like the Anderson Impurity Model when driven out of equilibrium. The authors introduce a novel mapping that rewrites the interacting dynamics as an effective, non-interacting Gaussian theory coupled to auxiliary degrees of freedom. This allows researchers to analyze complex many-body physics by solving a mathematically simpler, albeit larger, single-particle problem.
main_problem: The core challenge is understanding the complex, time-evolving dynamics of strongly interacting quantum impurity models when driven out of equilibrium (quenched).
main_result: The authors demonstrate that this non-equilibrium AIM evolution can be exactly mapped onto a completely non-interacting effective Gaussian theory coupled to an auxiliary chain.
method: They employ advanced numerical techniques like DMRG/MPS and variational optimization, treating the parameters of the effective non-interacting model as variational variables fitted against time-dependent expectation values from the interacting system.
model_or_system: The study focuses on the Anderson Impurity Model (AIM), which describes local moments in quantum dots or correlated materials. The method maps its complex interaction dynamics onto a solvable, non-interacting Hamiltonian augmented by auxiliary degrees of freedom.
key_observables: Impurity occupation $\langle n_d(t) angle$, real-space site occupations $\langle n_j(t) angle$, and the spectral function $A(\omega)$.
important_parameters: Interaction strength ($U$), impurity level ($\epsilon_d$), quench parameters (initial vs. final potentials), and the size of the auxiliary chain ($M$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that an effective non-interacting description, parameterized by optimizing against time evolution data, can capture the full dynamics of the interacting system.
figures_summary: Figures compare spectral functions (A(omega)) and quench dynamics ($\langle n_d(t) angle$) between the true AIM and the optimized auxiliary chain representation, showing quantitative agreement for both equilibrium and non-equilibrium regimes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the complexity of out-of-equilibrium AIM dynamics to developing the mapping strategy via Green's function formalism (spectral domain), then applying this mapping iteratively by optimizing parameters against time-dependent expectation values in real space, culminating in validation across multiple observables.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful conceptual and computational tool for analyzing non-equilibrium quantum dynamics. By transforming an intractable interacting problem into a solvable non-interacting one (albeit larger), it offers new insights into information propagation and correlation physics beyond standard equilibrium methods.
